title: One Big Beautiful Bill
excerpt: What is in the bill, and why has it sparked so much debate? A look back at the July 2025 post.
author: Shari Explains
coverAlt: Original cover artwork for One Big Beautiful Bill
body:
## One Big Beautiful Bill. Let’s discuss

On July 4th 2025, President Trump signed the ‘One Big Beautiful Bill’ into law after Vice President J.D. Vance cast the tie-breaking vote in favor of the bill. Since this bill has been proposed, it has been deemed a widely unpopular piece of legislation. The question on many minds is, ‘What does the bill contain?’

## Background: It’s all in the details…

Texas Representative Jodey Arrington introduced One Big Beautiful Bill as H.R.1 to the House of Representatives on May 16th, 2025. H.R.1 passed the House on May 22nd, 2025 (215–214). The bill later passed through the Senate on July 1st, 2025 (51–50), with J.D. Vance casting the tie-breaking vote in favor of the bill. President Donald Trump signed the bill into law on July 4th, 2025. Trump set a deadline for the bill to be passed and signed into law by America’s Independence Day, which proved to be difficult as the Senate spent 26 hours debating the bill. The Big Beautiful Bill was unpopular with the Democrats, with Democratic reps and senators trying to slow down the bill’s legislative process by throwing procedural hurdles in its way. Every single Democratic representative and senator voted against this bill, with only 2 Republican representatives voting against the bill. American citizens don’t seem to like this bill as well. According to polls, this bill is one of the most unpopular pieces of legislation in recent years.

## Taxes: Beneficial for some, but not for all

This bill can be described as an extension of Trump’s 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA). The Bill makes the TCJA less restrictive on interest deductions, securing a permanent addition of the 2017 individual tax breaks. The bill still retains some of the limits on several itemized deductions within the TCJA (mortgage interests), as well as limiting the value of itemized deductions for the wealthy. If you partake in overtime work and make money from tips, the bill introduces tax exemptions for you. However, if you are working-class citizen, it is likely that taxes just might become harder to file in the coming years. The BBB further complicates the already confusing tax process, making taxpayers scratch heads with new rules and compliance costs that usually outweigh the potential benefits. Under the new law, 88% of seniors who receive Social Security benefits will not pay taxes on them. This tax break will accelerate the timeline in which the trust funds of those who participate will become insolvent.

## SNAP: The loss of SNAP benefits for millions…

SNAP provides essential support for low-income families, individuals (with and without disabilities), and seniors (above 60 years old). SNAP currently has around 40 million recipients, and according to an analysis by the Urban Institute, 5.3 million would lose around $25 per month in SNAP with the new legislation. On average, families would lose around $146 in SNAP. The new legislation would also require recipients aged 55–64 to work to receive their benefits, requiring parents with children 14 or older to do the same as well.

## Medicaid: Healthcare for me, but not for thee…

Like SNAP, Medicaid (AKA, Medi-Cal for Californians) is an essential program for low-income families and individuals. The new law approves almost $1 trillion in cuts to medical care. In the new legislation, Medicaid recipients are expected to work for at least 80 hours a month. These requirements are expected to go into effect as early as January 2027. The cuts made in the bill also affect hospitals, as many are expected to face financial strain due to these budget cuts. Citizens of Rural America are expected to struggle to most, to combat this the Senate added a $50B rural hospital fund (2027–2032) as a cushion.

## Student loans: 1 in 6 Americans have student loan debt…

Many use payment plans like SAVE, PAYE, IBR, and ICR. Unfortunately, these payment plans will be cut. Current enrollees have until July 1st 2028 to switch plans. Repayment plans are now simpler to pay off for students, but they are longer. The number of repayments has reduced from 7 to 2. But with the elimination of the Deferment for Economic Hardship, borrowers will not be permitted to pause payments. Pell Grants are no longer available for students who are on full-ride scholarships. Workforce Pell Grants are now permitted for short-term programs, with the enrollees needing to obtain credentials or credits after.

## Defense + immigration: Big bucks are being put into defense, especially ICE…

A central part of Trump’s political agenda is curbing the number of undocumented immigrants coming to the U.S. The Big Beautiful Bill provides a total of $350 billion for Trump’s immigration plans. $45 billion goes towards ICE and detention centers, with 100,000 new spots being added for detainees and 10,000 new ICE positions being added. Each new job comes with a $10k signing bonus. $10 billion grants are also being given to states that recognize and comply with ICE’s jurisdiction. The bill makes ICE the most funded defense agency in the country. The new legislation also funds the controversial Gold Dome (missile defense system) and increases funding for space programs, and moves the space shuttle discovery from Virginia to Texas.
